h1: How brand extensions and surrogate ads work for Indian beer brands
title: Surrogate Ads and Beer Brands in India | Craft Beer School
desc: Why Indian beer brands sell soda, water and music under the beer's name, how surrogate advertising works and why it is a risky route for a craft brewery.
teaser: You have seen beer brand logos on soda bottles and music festivals. That is not a coincidence.
standfirst: Indian beer brands have long put their names on soda, packaged water and events. Here is why, how regulators see it and what it means for a craft brewery thinking about its own brand.
sections:
India restricts direct advertising of alcohol. Television, print and many outdoor formats cannot carry ads for beer, whisky or other liquor. Similar restrictions reach other media too. Yet beer is a brand-driven product. Big brewers need people to know their names.

The answer the industry found was the brand extension: a non-alcoholic product sold under the same name as the beer. Club soda, packaged water, glassware, music CDs and events have all carried famous beer and liquor names. Ads for the extension are legal. Viewers see the same logo and colours and think of the beer. That practice is called surrogate advertising.

Regulators and courts have long known what surrogate ads are for. Rules on television advertising, consumer protection guidelines on misleading ads and the advertising industry's own self-regulatory code all address it. Guidelines issued in 2022 on misleading advertisements explicitly list surrogate advertising as prohibited. The broad test is whether the extension is a genuine product sold in meaningful volume, with its own identity, or a vehicle for promoting the alcohol brand.

We are not lawyers. The details change, so treat this as background. If you plan anything in this space, take legal advice first. Our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India gives the wider picture.

Regulators tend to look at whether the extension behaves like a real business. Questions that come up include:

  • Is it actually sold in stores, in volumes that make sense?
  • Does the ad spend look reasonable against its sales?
  • Does the ad look like it promotes the soda or water, or the beer?
  • Does the extension have its own design, or is it a copy of the beer pack?

None of this is a checklist that makes an ad safe. It explains why regulators and courts have treated some campaigns as surrogate ads and others as legitimate.
Why it matters to a craft brewery

Most craft breweries will never run a television campaign, so surrogate ads may seem irrelevant. The same logic reaches smaller things, though: an alcohol-free version of your flagship, branded merchandise, a sponsored event or an influencer post that mentions a soda but shows a taproom. All of them can raise the same question about what is really being promoted.

For a small brand, the risk is not only a notice from a regulator. A craft brewery's reputation rests on being honest about what it makes. A campaign that looks like a workaround can cost more trust than it buys.
Extensions that make sense on their own

Some extensions are good business with no advertising angle. A brewpub that sells its own merchandise, glassware or spent grain snacks is building revenue and community. An alcohol-free beer that drinkers genuinely want is a real product. The test we suggest is simple: would you still make this if you could not advertise it? If yes, it is probably an extension worth having. If the only reason is the ad, think again.

Our guide to branded house or house of brands explains how to decide whether a new product should carry the brewery name at all.
Building a brand without the shortcut

Craft breweries in India mostly grow through the places they are allowed to speak: the taproom, the pack, their own social channels within the rules, word of mouth and events where drinkers already gather. These are slower than a television campaign. They also build a brand people feel they found themselves, which suits craft beer better than a borrowed logo on a soda bottle ever could.

Practical steps help here. Keep everything you publish clearly adult in tone. Gate your website and social pages for age where the platform allows. Avoid any suggestion that beer brings success, strength or popularity. Write these rules into your brand book so freelancers and agencies follow them too. None of this stops a brewery from being lively and funny. It simply keeps the fun on the right side of the line.

Where you stand in the drinker's mind matters more than where your logo appears. That is a positioning question. It is worth answering before any extension is on the table.
faqs: It is advertising a non-alcoholic product, such as soda or water, under an alcohol brand's name so the ad effectively promotes the alcohol. Indian consumer protection guidelines treat it as prohibited.
Can a brewery sell merchandise with its logo?
Generally yes. Selling genuine merchandise is common. How you advertise it is where care is needed, so take advice before any campaign.
Is an alcohol-free beer a surrogate product?
Not by nature. A genuine product sold on its own merits is different from an extension created mainly to advertise the alcoholic brand. Take advice before promoting it in channels alcohol cannot use.
